questions.q: A district lays an oil and gas pipeline beside a highway and puts a telecom tower next to it. Of the two, the pipeline belongs to ___ infrastructure.
questions.a: energy

questions.q: A dairy in a small town sells milk to a city 90 km away. The road is good and the trucks run daily, but power cuts of ten hours a day stop the cooling tanks. Using the chapter's 'pieces of a puzzle' idea, what follows?
questions.a: Satish's tomatoes needed canals, pumps, roads, cold storage and the internet working together; if one piece fails the others lose value. The wrong options say roads alone decide trade, that power does not touch business, or that electricity is not infrastructure; utilities such as electricity are part of physical infrastructure.
o: The roads lose much of their value because one linked piece, electricity, has failed
Nothing changes for the dairy, because good roads alone decide whether a business can trade
Only households suffer, since electricity is a utility meant for homes and has no link to trade
The dairy should build more roads first, because electricity is not counted as physical infrastructure

questions.q: Satish has good roads, canals and cold storage, but his village has no mobile or internet signal. Which help from his own account does he lose?
questions.a: In Satish's account the internet helped him know the best inputs and market prices. Canals and pumps gave irrigation, roads carried the trucks and cold storage kept the tomatoes fresh, so those three are still working.
o: Knowing the best inputs and the market prices for his crop
Canal and electric pump water for irrigating his tomato fields
Cold storage that keeps his tomatoes fresh until they are sold
Good roads that let trucks carry his tomatoes to the city

questions.q: Each year the apple growers of a hill village could not reach the city market for four months because the only path was washed away. A new all-weather road is built. Within two years a clinic opens, traders reach the village and homestays welcome tourists. Which statement from the chapter sums up this change?
questions.a: A new road connects a remote village and the chapter says this supports trade and tourism. The second option misreads the chapter's point that access itself supports tourism; the others use 'only' and 'do not help', which the chapter never claims.
o: Infrastructure joins remote areas and supports trade and tourism
A road matters mostly to car owners, so tourism depends on hotels and not on access
Infrastructure benefits only the defence forces in difficult terrain
Roads are useful for farmers but do not help hospitals reach people

questions.q: Heavy rain floods a district of Assam. Relief teams fly in food packets, and a phone alert tells people to move to higher ground. Which two parts of infrastructure helped in this emergency?
questions.a: Aircraft reach difficult places and mobile alerts warn people, so air transport and communication networks helped. Canals, cold storage, metro trains, solar parks and ports are real items in the chapter but were not used in this event.
o: Air transport and mobile networks
Cold storage rooms and irrigation canals
Metro trains and solar power projects
Expressways and container port cranes

questions.q:
Read the statements about physical infrastructure.
1. India has had a network of trade routes since ancient times, and modern infrastructure has taken this forward.
2. Better infrastructure helps the defence forces only on plains and not in other kinds of terrain.
3. Transport systems connect places where goods are made to the nearest markets.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says infrastructure improves access to all kinds of terrain for the defence forces, so 'only on plains' is wrong.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Physical infrastructure includes transportation, utilities, communication and energy infrastructure.
Reason (R): Better infrastructure strengthens national security by giving the defence forces access to all kinds of terrain.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: roads and railways, electricity and water pipelines, telephone lines and towers, and windmills and solar parks are examples of the four groups the chapter names. R is also true, but it speaks about security and does not explain what infrastructure includes.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each group of infrastructure in Column A with an example the chapter gives in Column B.
Column A: 1. Transportation  2. Utilities  3. Communication  4. Energy infrastructure
Column B: a. Telecom towers  b. Solar parks  c. Railways  d. Water pipelines
questions.a: Railways are transportation, water pipelines are utilities, telecom towers are communication and solar parks are energy infrastructure. The distractors swap utilities with energy, or transportation with communication.

questions.q: (a) A district builds a railway line, a water pipeline, a telephone tower and a solar park. Name the group of physical infrastructure each belongs to. (b) From Satish's account, give one example of one piece of infrastructure making another piece more useful.
questions.a: (a) Railway line: transportation; water pipeline: utilities; telephone tower: communication; solar park: energy infrastructure. (b) Any one: roads are useful only if cold storage keeps tomatoes fresh at the end; the internet is useful for market prices only if roads carry the tomatoes to that market.
s: Part (a): all four groups matched correctly
Part (b): a valid example of parts depending on each other

questions.q: (a) Name the four kinds of help that, in Satish's own account, got his tomatoes to the city: canals and pumps count as one kind. (b) If only the cold storage failed and everything else worked, what would most likely happen to his tomatoes, and why?
questions.a: (a) Canals and electric water pumps for irrigation, good roads for trucks, cold storage, and the internet for inputs and market prices. (b) They would lose freshness and could spoil before being sold, because cold storage is what kept them fresh.
s: Part (a): irrigation canals and pumps, roads, cold storage, internet
Part (b): tomatoes spoil because cold storage kept them fresh

questions.q: A newspaper writes, 'Telephone lines are utilities, just like water pipelines, because people use both every day.' (a) Correct the statement by naming the group each belongs to in the chapter. (b) Use the chapter's idea of the 'backbone' to say why a district must plan all the groups together.
questions.a: (a) Telephone lines belong to communication infrastructure (with the internet and telecom towers); water pipelines belong to utilities (with electricity). (b) Infrastructure is the backbone because it makes life easier for people and businesses and lets the government work smoothly, and its parts are connected like pieces of a puzzle, so a gap in one group weakens the others.
s: Part (a): telephone lines in communication, water pipelines in utilities
Part (b): backbone and parts connected, so plan them together

questions.q: True or False: Satish's tomatoes depended on four kinds of help (counting canals and pumps as one), so if the internet alone failed, his sale would not be affected because roads and cold storage would still work. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The internet gave him the best inputs and the market prices; without it he would lose that help even though trucks and cold storage worked, because the pieces of infrastructure work together like a puzzle.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the internet supplied inputs and price information, and every piece matters

questions.q: (a) Count the different modes of transport Rishabh used between his home in Delhi and his door in Talegaon, treating the car, metro, train, bus and autorickshaw as one mode each. (b) What does the number of changes show about how transport infrastructure must be arranged?
questions.a: (a) Five modes: car, metro, train, bus and autorickshaw. (b) The modes must connect at stations and stands so each change is easy, like pieces of a puzzle.
s: Part (a): five modes counted
Part (b): parts must connect with one another for a smooth journey

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'Infrastructure means only roads and railways, because only they carry people from place to place.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Roads and railways are only one group, transportation. The chapter also names utilities (electricity, water pipelines), communication (internet, telephone lines, towers) and energy infrastructure (windmills, solar parks, pipelines), and these keep homes, offices and farms working even though they carry no passengers.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'only'
Names at least two other groups with an example each
Explains that they keep cities and villages functioning

questions.q: Describe an imagined morning in a small town when one kind of infrastructure fails and makes two other kinds of infrastructure useless. Name the three kinds you use.
questions.a: Any valid story, e.g. a power cut stops electricity (utilities); the mobile tower (communication) and the electric water pump (utilities) stop with it, so the farmer cannot check the market price or irrigate. It shows that the parts depend on one another.
s: Names a failing infrastructure and two affected kinds
Shows the dependence between the parts in a logical way
Links the story to the idea that infrastructure works like pieces of a puzzle

questions.q: Match each situation with the benefit of infrastructure that the chapter names, and say how the infrastructure brings it: (i) a new rail line lets a shawl maker in Kullu sell in a city 800 km away; (ii) a new road lets army trucks reach a border post in the mountains; (iii) a new all-weather road lets tourists reach a remote lake village.
questions.a: (i) Trade: transport connects the place of manufacture to a distant market. (ii) National security: better access to all kinds of terrain for the defence forces. (iii) Tourism and connecting remote areas: easier access brings visitors to places that were hard to reach.
s: (i) trade, with the link to markets
(ii) security, access to all terrain
(iii) tourism or remote area access

questions.q: 'Physical infrastructure is the backbone of all other economic activities.' Justify this statement using Satish's tomatoes and at least two other ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Satish's tomatoes needed canals and pumps to grow, roads for trucks, cold storage for freshness and the internet for prices, so one activity (farming and selling) rests on four kinds of infrastructure. Transport joins makers to markets and boosts trade, as in the ancient trade routes. Infrastructure also supports tourism, connects remote areas and helps in floods and earthquakes. So quality infrastructure gives connectivity, jobs and ease of living.
s: Uses Satish's chain: irrigation, roads, cold storage, internet
First other idea: trade or ancient trade routes
Second other idea: tourism, remote areas, emergencies or security
Concludes: connectivity, employment and ease of living

questions.q: The Introduction asks you to imagine a school morning with no roads, no buses, no mobile signal, no electricity and no tap water. Explain what would go wrong in any four ways, name the group of infrastructure behind each, and then say which one a district should repair first after a flood and why.
questions.a: No roads or buses (transportation): the student and the groceries cannot reach school or the market. No signal or internet (communication): nobody can talk, work or learn online. No electricity (utilities): lights, pumps and appliances stop. No water (utilities): taps run dry. A valid priority, e.g. roads first because relief, ambulances and goods all travel on them, or power first because pumps and phones depend on it.
s: Four correct problems
Correct group of infrastructure named for each
Chooses one to repair first
Justifies the choice with a chapter idea

questions.q:
The panchayat of Chikhli, a village near Nashik, has ₹60 lakh to spend this year. Most of its farmers grow tomatoes, like Satish. The panchayat is considering four projects.
A: a 4.5 km all-weather road to the market at ₹8 lakh per km
B: a cold storage room for ₹24 lakh
C: a mobile tower for ₹12 lakh
D: repair of the canals for ₹18 lakh
(a) Find the cost of project A and name its group of infrastructure.
(b) Which pair of projects uses the whole ₹60 lakh exactly, and which two parts of Satish's chain from the chapter do these two projects supply?
(c) A sarpanch says project C is of no use to tomato growers. Using Satish's account, show why she is wrong.
(d) Recommend one pair of projects and justify it with the figures and one idea from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 4.5 x 8 = ₹36 lakh; transportation. (b) A and B (36 + 24 = 60); other pairs cost 48, 54, 36, 42 and 30 lakh. They supply good roads for trucks and cold storage. (c) In Satish's account the internet helped him know the best inputs and market prices, so a mobile tower serves the farmers. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: A + B (₹60 lakh, no balance) completes road plus cold storage of Satish's chain; A + C (₹48 lakh, ₹12 lakh left) adds market information and keeps a reserve.
s: Part (a): ₹36 lakh, transportation
Part (b): A and B, with roads and cold storage named from the chapter
Part (c): internet for inputs and market prices
Part (d): a pair chosen and justified with figures and a chapter idea

questions.q:
A hill village in Uttarakhand had 4 homestays and 1,200 tourists a year before an all-weather road was built. Five years later it has 14 homestays and 5,400 tourists a year. On average each tourist spends ₹2,500 in the village. The panchayat now wants to widen the road further, which would mean cutting a strip of forest. A clinic also opened in the village after the road came.
(a) Find how many more tourists come each year than before the road, and their extra yearly spending in lakh and in crore.
(b) Name the group of infrastructure the road belongs to and the kind the clinic belongs to.
(c) Name two kinds of villagers, other than homestay owners, who may gain indirectly.
(d) Should the panchayat widen the road through the forest? Give a reasoned decision using an idea from the chapter on infrastructure and the environment.
questions.a: (a) 5,400 - 1,200 = 4,200 more tourists; 4,200 x 2,500 = ₹1,05,00,000, i.e. ₹105 lakh or ₹1.05 crore. (b) The road is transportation infrastructure; the clinic is social infrastructure. (c) Any two: drivers, guides, shopkeepers, vegetable sellers, food stall owners (indirect benefits). (d) Either decision is accepted if reasoned: widen only if the forest loss is limited and the road is made sustainable, or do not widen because the chapter says infrastructure should minimise harm to bio-diversity and development and protection can go hand in hand.
s: Part (a): 4,200 tourists and ₹1.05 crore (105 lakh)
Part (b): transportation and social infrastructure
Part (c): two kinds of indirect beneficiaries
Part (d): a decision tied to the environment idea in the chapter

questions.q: Which statement about bridges in the chapter is NOT correct?
questions.a: Living root bridges are made from the roots of the Ficus elastica, the Indian rubber tree, guided across streams with bamboo and palm trunks. Naming the banyan is the error; the other three statements are in the chapter.
o: Living root bridges are made by the Khasi and Jaintia from banyan roots
The Dhola Sadiya Bridge crosses the Lohit River, a tributary of the Brahmaputra
Before the Dhola Sadiya Bridge, ferries did not work during floods
Some living root bridges take decades or even centuries to mature

questions.q: The Dhola Sadiya Bridge cut travel time by four hours. A vegetable van that crosses the Lohit River over it three times in a day now saves ___ hours of travel time that day.

A new national highway is planned to pass within 2 km of a port and a railway goods yard, but the plan has no link roads to either. A student calls this a design weakness. Which idea from the chapter supports her?
questions.a: The chapter says national highways and expressways connect with other infrastructure such as railway stations, airports and ports so that goods and people can travel smoothly. The other options give the job to the wrong government, split goods from people, or treat joining cities as enough, none of which the chapter says.
o: Highways should link up with railway stations, airports and ports
State governments, not the centre, must plan roads that serve ports and railway yards
Expressways are meant to carry people only, while ports and yards handle goods alone
A highway counts as complete once it joins cities, whatever lies along its route

questions.q: After heavy rain, a pothole is reported on a state highway joining two district towns and another on a national highway. A student writes, 'Both roads lie inside the state, so the state government must repair both.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: The chapter says state highways are built and maintained by the state, while national highways and expressways are built and maintained by the central government. So the state repairs the first and the central government the second. The other options give both to one government or flip them.
o: The state repairs the state highway and the central government repairs the national highway
The central government repairs the state highway and the state repairs the national highway
The central government repairs both roads
The student is right, since a road inside a state is always the state's

questions.q: Meena's village in Assam lies across a wide river. In the rainy season the ferry stops, vegetables spoil before reaching the market and patients wait for days. Which solution from the chapter fits this problem?
questions.a: The Dhola Sadiya Bridge replaced ferries that failed in floods and gave year-round travel. The chapter says highways cannot be built in wide river beds, and the Golden Quadrilateral links four metro cities and not this village.
o: A year-round bridge like Dhola Sadiya
A highway laid along the wide river bed
A longer timetable for the ferry in the monsoon
A new stretch of the Golden Quadrilateral

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Living root bridges are made by cutting down Ficus elastica trees and building with their timber.
Reason (R): The Khasi and Jaintia guide the roots across streams with bamboo and palm trunks, and the roots grow stronger over many years.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: R is true: the bridges are grown from living roots. A is false because no trees are cut for timber; the bridge itself is the living root structure.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Statement I: The Dhola Sadiya Bridge is the longest bridge in India.
Statement II: It connects Assam and Arunachal Pradesh across the Lohit River.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: At 9.15 km the bridge is the second longest in India, so Statement I is false. Statement II is true; the bridge links Assam and Arunachal Pradesh.
o: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Both statements are false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about roads in India.
1. India has the largest road network in the world, ahead of the USA.
2. Highways cannot be built everywhere, so bridges and tunnels are used in dense forests, wide river beds and steep mountains.
3. The Golden Quadrilateral joins Srinagar and Kanyakumari.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 2 is in the chapter. India has the second-largest road network after the USA, and the Golden Quadrilateral joins Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; Srinagar to Kanyakumari is NH44.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says highways can be built everywhere, so bridges and tunnels are needed only to shorten a journey. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says highways cannot be built everywhere, especially in dense forests, wide river beds and steep mountains, and in such places bridges and tunnels are what give ease of access.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: highways cannot be built in forests, river beds and mountains, so bridges and tunnels give access

questions.q: A truck leaves Srinagar for Kanyakumari along the national highway that runs the whole length of India and covers 400 km each day. (a) Recall the length of this highway and find the number of days the truck needs, counting a part day as a full day. (b) How many km are still left at the end of the tenth day?
s: Part (a): 4,112 km and 11 days
Part (b): 112 km left

questions.q: (a) A living root bridge near a village in Meghalaya is only 30 years old and still thin. According to the chapter, what will happen to it over the coming decades? (b) What is such a bridge called in the Khasi language, and from which tree is it made?
questions.a: (a) The roots will keep growing and become stronger, twisting into a natural bridge; some take decades or even centuries to mature and can last hundreds of years. (b) Jingkieng jri, from the Ficus elastica (Indian rubber tree).
s: Part (a): the roots grow stronger over the years
Part (b): jingkieng jri and Ficus elastica

questions.q: (a) Name the three kinds of difficult terrain where, according to the chapter, highways cannot be built everywhere. (b) A road must reach a village beyond a wide river bed and another beyond a steep mountain. Name the structure that suits each.
questions.a: (a) Dense forests, wide river beds and steep mountains. (b) A bridge for the wide river bed and a tunnel for the steep mountain, which give ease of access where a highway cannot be laid.
s: Part (a): all three terrains
Part (b): bridge for the river bed and tunnel for the mountain

questions.q: (a) A pothole appears on a state highway between two district towns and another on NH44. Which government must repair each? (b) For each of these, name the level of road and the government that maintains it: the lane to a farmer's field, the road joining two district towns, and the road joining two states.
questions.a: (a) The state government (public works department) repairs the state highway; the central government repairs NH44. (b) The lane to the field is a local road (kept up locally); the road joining district towns is a state highway (state government); the road joining states is a national highway (central government).
s: Part (a): state government for the state highway, central government for NH44
Part (b): local road, state highway and national highway matched with the right government

questions.q: Imran says, 'The Dhola Sadiya Bridge saved only four hours, so the old ferry across the Lohit River was nearly as good and the 9.15 km bridge was not needed.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The ferry did not work during floods, so travel stopped for days. The bridge gives year-round travel, so farmers can reach the market before vegetables spoil and people can reach hospitals even in floods, which matters far more than the four hours saved on an ordinary day.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Ferries failed during floods but the bridge gives year-round travel
Gains: farmers' vegetables and hospital access even in floods

questions.q: Compare the Dhola Sadiya Bridge and a living root bridge on any three points: where it is and what it crosses, its size, and what it gives the people who use it.
questions.a: Dhola Sadiya Bridge: connects Assam and Arunachal Pradesh across the Lohit River; 9.15 km long, the second longest in India; gives year-round travel and cuts travel time by four hours. Living root bridge: in Meghalaya, crafted by the Khasi and Jaintia over streams; stands 15-30 m high; is a living structure with cultural meaning, connecting one generation to another. Any three correct contrasts earn the marks.
s: First correct contrast
Second correct contrast
Third correct contrast

questions.q: A news website writes that NH44 (4,112 km) is about a quarter of the whole national highway network of India, which is about 150,000 km. Show with a calculation why this cannot be correct.
questions.a: A quarter of 150,000 km is 37,500 km, which is about nine times NH44's 4,112 km. Working the other way, 4,112 / 150,000 x 100 is about 2.7 per cent, far from 25 per cent.
s: States both lengths from the chapter
Finds a quarter of the network (37,500 km) or the share
Shows NH44 is only about 2.7 per cent and concludes the claim is impossible

questions.q: A town council wants to replace an old living root bridge in Meghalaya with a concrete bridge because it would be faster to cross. Evaluate the proposal using what the chapter says about how such bridges are made, how long they last, and what they mean to local people. End with your own recommendation.
questions.a: The bridge is made by the Khasi and Jaintia, who guide the roots of the Ficus elastica across a stream with bamboo and palm trunks, and the roots grow stronger over many years. It can take decades or even centuries to mature, and it can last for hundreds of years, so it is a durable structure that grows stronger rather than wearing out. It is also a reflection of the local people's knowledge of Nature and connects one generation to another, so a concrete replacement would lose a cultural meaning besides a path. A balanced recommendation, e.g. keep the living bridge and add a concrete bridge nearby only if travel needs really require it, earns the last mark.
s: Who makes it and how (roots, bamboo and palm trunks)
Time to mature and how long it lasts
Local knowledge of Nature
Cultural meaning: connects one generation to another
A reasoned recommendation that weighs speed against these gains

questions.q: A truck carries wheat from a village field to a railway station and a port in another state. Trace its journey in three stages, naming the level of road at each stage and the government that builds and maintains it, and then explain why the chapter says the highways connect with railway stations, airports and ports.
questions.a: Stage 1: a local road near the village carries the wheat to the town (such roads help farmers carry crops to markets). Stage 2: a state highway joins the town to other towns and districts within the state; it is built and maintained by the state through its public works department. Stage 3: a national highway or expressway takes it across states; it is built and maintained by the central government. The highways connect with railway stations, airports and ports so that goods and people can travel smoothly from one kind of transport to another, as in a chain.
s: Stage 1: local road and its use
Stage 2: state highway, built and maintained by the state
Stage 3: national highway or expressway, built and maintained by the central government
Links with railway stations, airports and ports named
Explains smooth movement of goods between modes

questions.q:
Class VII students of a school in Jorhat, Assam, study how a district's road system is organised. A list gives three trips taken by the school bus in a month, with the distance of each trip.
Trip 1: school to the market lane, 6 km on a local road
Trip 2: school to the district headquarters, 55 km on a state highway
Trip 3: school to a city across the state border, 120 km on a national highway
(a) Which government builds and maintains the road used on trip 2, and which the road used on trip 3?
(b) Recall the length of NH44, the longest national highway. About how many times as long is it as trip 3?
(c) Their teacher says that a fourth trip, from Assam into Arunachal Pradesh across the Lohit River, is now possible in every season. Name the structure that makes this possible and explain why it matters to travellers.
(d) The school can afford only one trip per term. Which trip would you plan, trip 2 or trip 3, so that children also learn about how the roads connect to other infrastructure? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Trip 2: the state government through its public works department; trip 3: the central government. (b) NH44 is 4,112 km; 4,112 / 120 = about 34.3 times. (c) The Dhola Sadiya Bridge (Bhupen Hazarika Setu). Before it, travel across the Lohit depended on ferries, which did not work during floods; the bridge gives year-round travel and cuts travel time by four hours. (d) Either trip with a reason: trip 3 on a national highway, which connects with railway stations, airports and ports, or trip 2, a state highway linking towns within the state at less cost.
s: Part (a): state government and central government
Part (b): 4,112 km and about 34.3 times
Part (c): names the bridge and says ferries failed in floods while the bridge gives year-round travel
Part (d): a trip chosen with a chapter-based reason

questions.q:
Roshan runs a vegetable transport business in Assam with 6 trucks that cross a river to a city market once each per day. Suppose a bridge like Dhola Sadiya cuts every crossing by the same number of hours as that bridge did. Each truck costs ₹450 for every hour it is on the road. Before the bridge the ferry ran on 335 days a year and the river was in flood on the other 30 days. He wants to spend on one item: a cold storage room for ₹9 lakh that prevents spoilage worth ₹9,000 a day, but only in the 150-day vegetable season; or a seventh truck for ₹11 lakh that now earns ₹9,500 a day net on all 365 days, since the bridge never closes.
(a) By how many hours does the bridge cut each crossing?
(b) Find Roshan's daily saving on the 6 trucks.
(c) Find the saving over the 335 days when the ferry ran, and say what happened to his business on the 30 flood days before the bridge.
(d) Find the days of working each item takes to repay its cost and its gain in the first year after the cost is repaid out of the year's earnings. Then recommend one, giving a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Four hours. (b) 6 x 4 x 450 = ₹10,800 a day. (c) 10,800 x 335 = ₹36,18,000 (₹36.18 lakh). On flood days the ferry did not work, so the trucks could not cross and vegetables spoiled. (d) Cold storage repays in 9,00,000 / 9,000 = 100 working days; the truck in 11,00,000 / 9,500 = about 116 days. In one year cold storage earns 9,000 x 150 = ₹13.5 lakh, a first-year gain of ₹4.5 lakh; the truck earns 9,500 x 365 = ₹34,67,500, a gain of about ₹23.7 lakh. So cold storage repays sooner and keeps vegetables fresh on the way to the market, as in Satish's chain, but the truck gains far more in a year and uses the bridge that now stays open in floods. Either is accepted if the recommendation uses both the payback and the first-year gain and gives a chapter reason (storage and fresh produce, or reliable all-year links).
s: Part (a): 4 hours
Part (b): ₹10,800 a day
Part (c): ₹36.18 lakh, and ferry did not run in floods
Part (d): paybacks 100 and about 116 days, first-year gains, and a reasoned recommendation

questions.q: A school quiz lists four locomotives in a jumbled way: WAM-4 (electric, 1970), F-734 (steam, 1895), Vande Bharat (electric, 2019) and WDM-1 (diesel, 1957). Which option puts them in the order in which they entered service, as in the chapter's timeline?
questions.a: Sorting by year gives F-734 (1895), WDM-1 (1957), WAM-4 (1970) and Vande Bharat (2019). The other orders put the electric WAM-4 before the diesel WDM-1, or start with the diesel.
o: F-734, WDM-1, WAM-4, Vande Bharat
WDM-1, F-734, WAM-4, Vande Bharat
F-734, WAM-4, WDM-1, Vande Bharat
WAM-4, WDM-1, F-734, Vande Bharat

questions.q: Fig. 7.8 in the chapter gives the percentage of railway network electrified in 2024: India 97, China 75, France 61, Germany 55 and the United Kingdom 38. Which of the following statements is NOT supported by these figures?
questions.a: China's share (75) is lower than India's (97), so saying it is higher is not supported. India's 97 is more than 2.5 times the United Kingdom's 38, France is above Germany, and every country shown has more than a third electrified.
o: China has a higher share than India
India's share is more than 2.5 times the United Kingdom's
France has a higher share than Germany

questions.a: Samuel Morse invented the telegraph (1844), Bell the telephone (1876), Bain the fax machine (1843) and J.C. Bose a new type of coherer. The distractors swap the telegraph and telephone inventors or give the coherer to Bain.

questions.q: (a) A school in a remote hill village has no Physics teacher. Name two resources from the chapter that communication infrastructure can bring to its students. (b) A cyclone is expected and officials must warn villagers within minutes. Name the tool the chapter mentions for this.
questions.a: (a) Any two of online classes, digital libraries and educational videos. (b) Quick mobile SMS alerts or apps.
s: Part (a): two educational resources
Part (b): SMS alerts or apps for emergency response

questions.q: True or False: The fax machine (1843) came 33 years before the telephone (1876), and the telegraph (1844) was invented after the fax machine. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The fax machine was invented in 1843 by Alexander Bain, the telegraph in 1844 by Samuel Morse and the telephone in 1876 by Alexander Graham Bell; 1876 - 1843 = 33 years.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: dates 1843, 1844 and 1876, with the difference of 33 years

questions.q: A pensioner in a village downloads her documents from DigiLocker instead of travelling 40 km to a government office. (a) Is this e-commerce or e-governance, and why? (b) The bus fare is ₹60 each way. How much does she save over 12 such visits in a year?
questions.a: (a) E-governance, because the government delivers a service to a citizen through communication technology; DigiLocker is the chapter's example. (b) 60 x 2 x 12 = ₹1,440.
s: Part (a): e-governance, with the reason

questions.q: (a) Classify each as e-commerce or e-governance: a farmer sells jaggery on a website; a citizen files a complaint online with the government. (b) What do both depend on, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Selling jaggery online is e-commerce; filing a complaint online with the government is e-governance. (b) Both depend on communication infrastructure and technologies such as the internet.
s: Part (a): both classified correctly
Part (b): communication infrastructure or technology such as the internet

questions.q: Arrange the following in order, earliest first: television, telegraph, internet, telephone. Give the year of the earliest and the latest, and the number of years between them.
questions.a: Telegraph (1844), telephone (1876), television (1927), internet (1994). The earliest is 1844 and the latest is 1994, which are 150 years apart.
s: Correct order of the four
Years of the earliest and latest, and the gap of 150 years

questions.q: Describe the stages Rani's voice note passes through on its way from her phone in a village in Madhya Pradesh to her cousin's phone in Tamil Nadu, and say what would stop if the electricity failed at the first tower.
questions.a: Electricity powers the tower near her village, which receives the note; it then travels through fibre cables under fields and roads, to satellites, and to giant servers, and finally reaches her cousin's phone. If the first tower lost electricity the note could not start its journey, and every later stage would receive nothing.
s: Stages in the chapter's order: powered tower, fibre cables, satellites, servers, cousin's phone
Role of each stage described
Failure at the first tower stops the whole journey

questions.q: An old relative says that in the 1990s he paid only ₹9,000 for a month of 30-minute calls every day at the top mobile rate. Using the chapter's rate, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The top rate was ₹17 per minute. A 30-minute call every day for 30 days is 30 x 30 = 900 minutes, which costs 900 x 17 = ₹15,300. This is more than ₹9,000, so his figure cannot be right at the top rate.
s: Uses ₹17 per minute
Computes 900 minutes and ₹15,300
Compares with ₹9,000 and concludes

questions.q: Kabir says, 'The chapter's text dates J.C. Bose's Calcutta experiment to 1895, while its timeline shows his wireless demonstration under 1899. Either way it came before Marconi's patent of 1901, so Bose deserves recognition as an early pioneer of wireless transmission even though Marconi won the Nobel Prize.' Do you agree? Use dates from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. On either date Bose came first: 1901 - 1895 = 6 years before Marconi's patent by the text, or 1901 - 1899 = 2 years by the timeline. Bose showed signals passing through a wall and invented a new type of coherer. Marconi patented a similar device in 1901 and won the Nobel Prize in 1909, but Bose rarely bothered to patent his inventions, which explains why his work did not gain international recognition even though the early work was his.
s: Verdict: agrees, because both dates in the chapter (1895 and 1899) fall before 1901
Bose's coherer and demonstration; Marconi's patent and Nobel Prize
Rarely patented, so less recognition

questions.q: A classmate says, 'J.C. Bose got less credit than Marconi because his science was weaker.' Evaluate this claim using five points from the chapter on what Bose did, what Marconi did and why recognition differed.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. Bose pioneered wireless transmission using microwaves in the millimetre range and showed in 1895 in Calcutta that signals could pass through a wall. He invented a new type of coherer, a galena crystal detector, antennas and waveguides. Marconi patented a similar device in 1901, sent a radio signal across the Atlantic the same year and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909. The chapter says Bose rarely bothered to patent his inventions, which did not help them gain international recognition, although he received several honours, including for plant physiology, and created the Bose Institute in 1917.
s: Bose's 1895 experiment and microwaves
Bose's devices such as the coherer
Marconi's patent in 1901 and Nobel Prize in 1909
Bose rarely patented, so recognition was less
A verdict that the claim is not supported, with honours or the Bose Institute

questions.q: A museum panel must show five milestones of communication in order and explain how each made communication faster or wider than the one before it. Choose five milestones from the chapter's timelines, give each year, and write the improvement in one line each.
questions.a: One acceptable set, earliest first: the telegraph (1844) sent electric signals over long distances by dots and dashes, faster than runners or horse couriers; the telephone (1876) carried the voice itself; television (1927) brought moving pictures to homes; the smartphone (1993) put calling and computing in one hand; the internet (1994) joined computers across the world. Other correct milestones with correct years are accepted if the order is right and each improvement is explained.
s: Five valid milestones
Correct years for them
Correct order, earliest first
Improvement over the earlier method explained for at least three
Improvement explained for all five

questions.q:
A village panchayat in Odisha keeps a record of five flood-prone villages. It plans to warn people of floods through quick alerts to their phones, each message costing ₹0.20, for 3 rounds of warning. Assume one phone belongs to one person.
Village A: 3,200 people, 2,400 phones
Village B: 1,800 people, 1,100 phones
Village C: 4,100 people, 3,000 phones
Village D: 950 people, 300 phones
Village E: 2,500 people, 1,700 phones
(a) Name the use of communication in a disaster that this plan shows, according to the chapter. Which village will gain least from it, and what share of its people has phones?
(b) Find the total cost of 3 rounds of messages to all phones.
(c) How many people in the five villages have no phone to receive the alert?
(d) ₹40,000 is left. Plan X: loudspeaker sirens in village D only, costing ₹15,000. Plan Y: ₹8,000 each for a community alert centre in every village. Choose one and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Quick mobile alerts (SMS or apps) support emergency response; village D, where 300 of 950 people (31.6 per cent) have phones. (b) Total phones = 8,500; 8,500 x 3 x 0.20 = ₹5,100. (c) Total people 12,550; 12,550 - 8,500 = 4,050 people. (d) Plan X costs ₹15,000 and leaves ₹25,000, but helps only village D, which has the weakest coverage (68.4 per cent without phones); Plan Y costs 5 x 8,000 = ₹40,000, uses all the money and reaches every village, where 25 to 68 per cent have no phone. Either is accepted if tied to the figures and the chapter's idea of communication in disasters.
s: Part (a): SMS alerts for emergency response; village D at about 31.6 per cent
Part (c): 4,050 people
Part (d): an option chosen and justified using the figures

questions.q:
The history club of a Kolkata school prepares a wall timeline titled 'Who gave us wireless?'. It must fix the dates for four panels: the telegraph, the telephone, Bose's experiment in Calcutta and Marconi's patent.
(a) How many years after the telegraph was the telephone invented?
(b) Use 1895, the year the chapter's text gives for Bose's Calcutta experiment. How many years separate it from Marconi's patent (1901)?
(c) Marconi won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909. How many years after Bose's 1895 experiment was this?
(d) The club must give the title panel to either Bose or Marconi. Choose one and justify with two points from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Telegraph 1844, telephone 1876: 32 years. (b) Bose 1895 (the chapter's text; its timeline shows 1899, which would give 2 years), Marconi patent 1901: 6 years. (c) 1909 - 1895 = 14 years. (d) Either is accepted with two valid points: Bose showed signals passing through a wall in 1895 and invented a coherer; Marconi patented a similar device in 1901, sent a radio signal across the Atlantic the same year and won the Nobel Prize in 1909, while Bose rarely patented.
s: Part (a): 32 years
Part (b): 6 years
Part (c): 14 years
Part (d): a choice with two points from the chapter

questions.q: A councillor's report must list only the social infrastructure of her town. Which list should she submit?
questions.a: Hospitals, libraries and fire stations are all social infrastructure. Every other list has an intruder: solar parks are energy, telephone lines are communication and bridges are transportation infrastructure.
o: Hospitals, libraries and fire stations
Hospitals, solar parks and courts
Schools, telephone lines and parks
Police stations, bridges and community centres

questions.q: A 250 m stretch of city road built to the Arthashastra width given in the chapter covers ___ square metres.
A museum builds a model township using the Arthashastra widths in the chapter (simplified to metres). It needs a road to a port town, a forest road and a chariot road. Which set of widths is right?
questions.a: The chapter gives 16 m for roads in port towns (as for royal highways, countryside roads and roads to villages), 8 m for forest roads and roads within the city, and 2.5 m for chariot roads. The other sets mix up these widths.
o: 16 m, 8 m and 2.5 m
16 m, 16 m and 8 m
8 m, 8 m and 2.5 m
8 m, 2.5 m and 16 m

questions.q: Sunita notices a broken streetlight on the lane to her school and phones the municipal office, which repairs it in two days. Which idea from the chapter does her action show?
questions.a: The chapter says individuals should use infrastructure responsibly and report damage like potholes or broken streetlights. The other options use 'alone' or claim something the chapter does not say.
o: Citizens should report damage like broken streetlights
The government alone is responsible for public infrastructure
Penalties alone are enough to protect public infrastructure
Social infrastructure replaces the need for physical infrastructure

questions.q: A town plans a new bus stand. Which feature best follows the chapter's idea that infrastructure should be designed for everyone?
questions.a: The chapter says design should consider the needs of children, the elderly and disabled persons. Solar panels are a good sustainability feature but do not address that point, and the other two ideas are not in the chapter.
o: Ramps, seats and signs for the elderly, children and disabled
Solar panels across the whole roof to reduce emissions and cost
A very wide car park at the front entrance for visitors' cars
Shops on every platform so that the town earns more rent

questions.q:
Statement I: The Arthashastra gave no punishments for damage to waterworks.
Statement II: It suggested a severe penalty for breaking the dam of a reservoir.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Arthashastra deterred damage to infrastructure with punishments and fines and recommended a severe penalty for those damaging waterworks, such as breaking a reservoir dam. So Statement I is false and Statement II is true.
o: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Both statements are true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Both statements are false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about public infrastructure.
1. Taking care of public infrastructure is the duty of the government alone.
2. Solar panels on buildings can help reduce emissions.
3. The Arthashastra recommended fines for those who broke the hedge to trespass into public parks.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the chapter calls it a collective responsibility in which the role of citizens is equally important.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Writing on monuments and littering roads reduce the ease of living of people.
Reason (R): The Arthashastra recommended fines for those who broke the hedge to trespass into public parks.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are in the chapter. The Arthashastra's fine is a historical rule about deterring damage; it says nothing about why defacing monuments or littering roads lowers ease of living, so R is true but does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A town builds a footbridge with steep steps and no ramp, using materials that pollute heavily. (a) Whose needs does the chapter say the design should have considered? (b) Suggest one change, from the chapter, that would also cut pollution.
questions.a: (a) Children, the elderly and disabled persons. (b) Use cleaner energy such as solar panels for lighting, or environment-friendly materials, to minimise pollution and harm to bio-diversity.
s: Part (a): children, the elderly and disabled persons
Part (b): cleaner energy or environment-friendly materials

questions.q: (a) A new town has roads, power lines, a mobile tower, a hospital and a school. Which two of these are social infrastructure? (b) How does social infrastructure support the town in a way that the roads and power lines do not?
questions.a: (a) The hospital and the school. (b) It supports the wellbeing and development of the community and society (health, learning), while the roads and power lines are physical structures for movement and supply.
s: Part (a): hospital and school
Part (b): supports wellbeing and development of communities

questions.q: (a) A city road and a chariot road are laid side by side under the Arthashastra widths in the chapter. Find their combined width. (b) How many times as wide as the chariot road is the city road?
s: Part (a): 10.5 m
Part (b): 3.2 times

questions.q: A student breaks a bench in a public park. Why does the chapter say such damage is a problem for everybody and not only for the park staff?
questions.a: Damage to public infrastructure reduces ease of living for people and becomes a burden for every citizen. Taking care of it is therefore a collective responsibility.
s: Damage reduces ease of living and burdens every citizen
Hence care is a collective responsibility

questions.q: (a) Ravi notices a pothole outside his school and Neha sees a classmate writing on a monument wall. What does the chapter expect each of them to do? (b) Why is it not enough to wait for the authorities alone?
questions.a: (a) Ravi should report the pothole to the authorities; Neha should use public infrastructure responsibly and not write on monuments (and discourage it). (b) The chapter says the role of citizens is equally important, since damage burdens every citizen and care is a collective responsibility.
s: Part (a): report the pothole; do not deface the monument
Part (b): citizens' role equally important; collective responsibility

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The Arthashastra shows that only the state looked after roads and waterways, and the villagers had no part in it.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The state did have a major role, with detailed rules on road widths and punishments, but the chapter says the state, grama and sabhas were actively involved in developing and maintaining roads and waterways, so 'only the state' is wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
State's role: rules and punishments
Grama and sabhas also involved, so 'only' is wrong

questions.q: Write three rules that a ward committee would put up on a notice board for citizens. Each rule must be tied to a different idea from the chapter: responsible use, reporting damage and inclusive design.
questions.a: For example: do not litter roads or stain buildings or monuments (responsible use); report potholes and broken streetlights to the municipal office (reporting damage); keep ramps and footpaths clear so children, the elderly and disabled persons can use them (inclusive design).
s: First rule tied to responsible use
Second rule tied to reporting damage
Third rule tied to inclusive design

questions.q: A newspaper says that widening a 5 km forest road from the Arthashastra's forest-road width of 8 m to its royal-highway width of 16 m would add only 10 per cent to the land the road uses. Show with calculations why this cannot be right.
questions.a: Forest roads were 8 m and royal highways 16 m. The land used is 5,000 m x 8 m = 40,000 sq m now and 5,000 x 16 = 80,000 sq m after widening. That is an increase of 100 per cent, not 10 per cent.
s: Uses 8 m and 16 m
Computes 40,000 and 80,000 sq m
Shows the increase is 100 per cent and rejects 10 per cent

questions.q: 'Taking care of public infrastructure is a collective responsibility.' Justify this statement using the damage described, the role of government and the role of citizens.
questions.a: Roads littered, buildings stained and monuments written on reduce ease of living and become a burden for every citizen, so the problem is shared. The government must improve waste management, sewers, traffic management, clean drinking water and footpaths, and can impose penalties, as the Arthashastra's fines did. Citizens are equally important: they must use infrastructure responsibly and report damage such as potholes and broken streetlights. So both together keep infrastructure safe and sustainable for children, the elderly and disabled persons.
s: Types of damage and burden on every citizen
Government services needed
Government penalties with a historical example
Citizens' duty to use responsibly and report
Conclusion tying the two together

questions.q: Compare how the Arthashastra and the chapter's account of modern India deal with protecting public infrastructure. Include who was involved, rules for roads and the punishments.
questions.a: In the Arthashastra, the state, grama and sabhas were actively involved in developing and maintaining roads and waterways. It gave detailed rules on road widths by traffic: 16 m for royal highways, 8 m for forest and city roads, and 2.5 m for chariot roads. It fined or severely punished damage, such as breaking a reservoir dam or breaking the hedge of a public park. In the chapter's modern India, Panchayats and municipalities provide services, the government can impose penalties, and citizens are expected to use infrastructure responsibly and report damage.
s: Who was involved in the Arthashastra
Road width rules with examples
Punishments and fines with examples
Modern roles of Panchayat, municipality and government
Role of citizens today and a clear comparison

questions.q:
The Nagpur school of a student named Pooja wants rooftop solar panels of 40 kW on its library block for ₹24 lakh. Each kW gives 4 units of electricity a day, the school runs 300 days a year and the electricity board charges ₹8 per unit. Another proposal would spend the same ₹24 lakh on ramps, a lift and accessible toilets so that 14 children with disabilities can use every floor.
(a) Name the kind of infrastructure the library and the solar panels are, and one environmental benefit of the panels given in the chapter.
(b) Find the yearly saving on the electricity bill.
(c) In how many years do the savings repay the cost of the panels?
(d) Choose one proposal, or a way to combine them, and justify it using the chapter's ideas on sustainable and inclusive design.
questions.a: (a) The library is social infrastructure and the panels are energy infrastructure; the panels use cleaner energy and reduce emissions. (b) 40 x 4 x 300 = 48,000 units; 48,000 x 8 = ₹3,84,000. (c) 24,00,000 / 3,84,000 = 6.25 years. (d) Any reasoned answer: panels repay in 6.25 years and cut emissions, but the chapter also says design must consider disabled persons, so the ramps may come first, or the school may do the ramps now and the panels next; both are acceptable if justified.
s: Part (a): social and energy infrastructure, with emissions reduced
Part (c): 6.25 years
Part (d): a justified choice using sustainable and inclusive design

questions.q:
The Ward 12 office of a town logs these complaints in one month and has ₹5 lakh to put right as many as it can.
Potholes on roads: 25 complaints, ₹6,000 to repair each
Broken streetlights: 40 complaints, ₹2,500 to repair each
Writing and stains on the community hall: 12 complaints, ₹3,000 to clean each
Overflowing sewer lines: 8 complaints, ₹35,000 to repair each
(a) Which two of these entries does the chapter name as damage that citizens should report?
(b) Find the cost of clearing every complaint in each row and the total.
(c) By how much does the total exceed the budget, and can leaving out the cleaning of the community hall alone fix this?
(d) The office must leave out one row. Choose which and justify it using the figures and an idea from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Potholes and broken streetlights. (b) Potholes 25 x 6,000 = ₹1,50,000; streetlights 40 x 2,500 = ₹1,00,000; community hall 12 x 3,000 = ₹36,000; sewers 8 x 35,000 = ₹2,80,000; total ₹5,66,000. (c) ₹66,000 over; leaving out the hall saves only ₹36,000, so it is not enough. (d) Leaving out potholes, streetlights or sewers each fits the budget (₹4,16,000, ₹4,66,000 or ₹2,86,000). Any choice is accepted if justified, for example leaving out streetlights because they are cheapest to postpone, or keeping sewers because the chapter lists sewer systems among services to improve.
s: Part (a): potholes and broken streetlights
Part (b): row costs and ₹5,66,000 total
Part (c): ₹66,000 over and the hall alone is not enough
Part (d): a row left out, justified with figures and the chapter
